sections.title: Daily remembrance basics
sections.intro: Start with a few short phrases you can understand and repeat easily. Dhikr is not a race, and nobody is counting.

entries.title: SubhanAllah
entries.occasion: Any time, and often after prayer
entries.meaning: Glory be to Allah.
entries.note: A short remembrance that turns your heart back toward Allah. Useful when your mind has wandered off.

entries.title: Alhamdulillah
entries.occasion: Gratitude, ordinary moments, and after prayer
entries.meaning: All praise belongs to Allah.
entries.note: Use it when you notice a blessing, large or small.

entries.title: Allahu Akbar
entries.meaning: Allah is the Greatest.
entries.note: Saying it puts your worries, and whoever you are worried about, back in proportion.

entries.title: La ilaha illa Allah
entries.meaning: There is no god worthy of worship except Allah.
entries.note: This is the heart of Islamic belief. Say it with attention, not as background noise.

sections.title: Before and after prayer
sections.intro: Prayer already holds the duas a beginner most needs. When you finish, sit for a moment with a short dhikr before you get up.

entries.title: Guidance from Al-Fatiha
entries.meaning: Guide us to the straight path.
entries.note: You say this in every rak'ah. If you learn the meaning of one line of prayer first, make it this one.

entries.title: After-prayer dhikr pattern
entries.arabic:
سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ
اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ
entries.meaning: Glorify Allah, praise Allah, and declare Allah's greatness.
entries.note: Many Muslims repeat these after every prayer. Start with a few of each and learn the full count later.

sections.title: Asking for guidance
sections.intro: Use these when you feel unsure, pulled in two directions, or worried that your faith will not hold.

entries.title: Keep my heart steady
entries.arabic: رَبَّنَا لَا تُزِغْ قُلُوبَنَا بَعْدَ إِذْ هَدَيْتَنَا وَهَبْ لَنَا مِن لَّدُنكَ رَحْمَةً
entries.transliteration: Rabbana la tuzigh qulubana ba'da idh hadaytana wa hab lana min ladunka rahmah
entries.meaning: Our Lord, do not let our hearts turn away after You have guided us, and grant us mercy from You.
entries.note: A Quranic dua for the days when you are afraid of slipping or losing the thread.

entries.title: Good in this life and the next
entries.arabic: رَبَّنَا آتِنَا فِي الدُّنْيَا حَسَنَةً وَفِي الْآخِرَةِ حَسَنَةً وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ
entries.transliteration: Rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanah wa fil-akhirati hasanah wa qina 'adhaban-nar
entries.meaning: Our Lord, give us good in this world and the Hereafter, and protect us from the Fire.
entries.note: A short Quranic dua that asks for good in the life you are living now and good in the one after it.

sections.title: When you feel anxious or overwhelmed
sections.intro: Dua and dhikr bring real comfort. They are not a substitute for help when you are in crisis, thinking of hurting yourself, being abused, or unable to get through the day.

entries.title: For anxiety and grief
entries.occasion: When worry, sadness, debt, or pressure feels heavy
entries.arabic: اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنَ الْهَمِّ وَالْحُزْنِ، وَالْعَجْزِ وَالْكَسَلِ، وَالْبُخْلِ وَالْجُبْنِ، وَضَلَعِ الدَّيْنِ وَغَلَبَةِ الرِّجَالِ
entries.transliteration: Allahumma inni a'udhu bika minal-hammi wal-huzn, wal-'ajzi wal-kasal, wal-bukhli wal-jubn, wa dala'id-dayn wa ghalabatir-rijal
entries.meaning: O Allah, I seek refuge in You from worry, grief, helplessness, laziness, miserliness, cowardice, heavy debt, and being overpowered.
entries.note: Say this, and also take the practical step in front of you: make the call, see the doctor, tell someone.

entries.title: Patience and firm steps
entries.occasion: Before a hard conversation or test
entries.arabic: رَبَّنَا أَفْرِغْ عَلَيْنَا صَبْرًا وَثَبِّتْ أَقْدَامَنَا
entries.transliteration: Rabbana afrigh 'alayna sabran wa thabbit aqdamana
entries.meaning: Our Lord, pour patience upon us and make our steps firm.
entries.note: A Quranic dua for the moment right before something hard, when you need patience and nerve at once.

sections.title: Gratitude and repentance
sections.intro: Repentance is not reserved for the big failures. It is an ordinary, regular return to Allah, done honestly and with hope.

entries.title: Sayyid al-istighfar
entries.occasion: Morning, evening, or after you have slipped
entries.arabic: اللَّهُمَّ أَنْتَ رَبِّي لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ، خَلَقْتَنِي وَأَنَا عَبْدُكَ، وَأَنَا عَلَى عَهْدِكَ وَوَعْدِكَ مَا اسْتَطَعْتُ، أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ شَرِّ مَا صَنَعْتُ، أَبُوءُ لَكَ بِنِعْمَتِكَ عَلَيَّ، وَأَبُوءُ بِذَنْبِي، فَاغْفِرْ لِي فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ
entries.transliteration: Allahumma anta Rabbi la ilaha illa ant, khalaqtani wa ana 'abduk, wa ana 'ala 'ahdika wa wa'dika mastata't...
entries.meaning: O Allah, You are my Lord. I admit Your blessings and my sins, so forgive me, for none forgives sins except You.
entries.note: This one is longer than a starter phrase. Learn it a line at a time and keep the meaning in front of you while you do.

entries.title: Forgiveness and mercy
entries.arabic: رَبَّنَا آمَنَّا فَاغْفِرْ لَنَا وَارْحَمْنَا وَأَنْتَ خَيْرُ الرَّاحِمِينَ
entries.transliteration: Rabbana amanna faghfir lana warhamna wa anta khayrur-rahimin
entries.meaning: Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy on us; You are the best of those who show mercy.
entries.note: A short Quranic dua that puts faith, forgiveness, and mercy into one sentence.

sections.title: Before learning or a hard conversation
sections.intro: Before you open a book, ask a question, or sit down with your family, ask Allah for clear understanding and gentle speech.

entries.title: Ease and an open heart
entries.occasion: Before learning, speaking, or asking for help
entries.arabic:
رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي
وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي
وَاحْلُلْ عُقْدَةً مِّن لِّسَانِي
يَفْقَهُوا قَوْلِي
entries.transliteration: Rabbi ishrah li sadri. Wa yassir li amri. Wahlul 'uqdatan min lisani. Yafqahu qawli.
entries.meaning: My Lord, open my heart, make my task easy, loosen the knot from my tongue, and let my words be understood.
entries.note: This is the dua of Prophet Musa, peace be upon him. Many new Muslims say it before a conversation they have been dreading.

entries.title: Beneficial knowledge
entries.arabic: اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ عِلْمًا نَافِعًا، وَرِزْقًا طَيِّبًا، وَعَمَلًا مُتَقَبَّلًا
entries.transliteration: Allahumma inni as'aluka 'ilman nafi'a, wa rizqan tayyiba, wa 'amalan mutaqabbala
entries.meaning: O Allah, I ask You for beneficial knowledge, good provision, and accepted deeds.
entries.note: Useful before a class on Islam, and just as useful before work, school, or learning a skill.

sections.title: Personal dua in your own words
sections.intro: You can call on Allah in the language you actually think in. Just keep your own wording separate in your mind from Quranic and Prophetic wording.

entries.title: Personal wording
entries.occasion: Any time outside fixed prayer recitation
entries.meaning: Example: O Allah, guide me, forgive me, make prayer easy for me, and place good people in my life.
entries.note: This is personal wording, not a transmitted dua. Ask Allah for what you need, in your own language, in your own words.

phrases.title: Everyday phrases: what they mean and how to reply
phrases.intro: Muslims around you will use these short Arabic phrases in ordinary conversation. Each card gives the meaning, when people say it, and the reply if there is one. Where the reply is common courtesy rather than wording from a hadith, the card says so.
tips: Learn three this week: the greeting and its reply, Bismillah, and Jazak Allahu khayran.
Add the sneeze reply and inna lillahi next. They come with a set reply or a sensitive moment.
If you forget the Arabic, say the meaning in English. It is still a kind and right thing to say.
Print this page or keep it open on your phone until the phrases come naturally.

entries.meaning: Peace be upon you.
entries.when: When you meet a Muslim, arrive at the masjid, enter a home or start a phone call.
entries.reply: Wa alaykum as-salam (and upon you be peace). You can add wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh (and the mercy of Allah and His blessings).
entries.note: The Quran asks you to answer a greeting with a better one or at least the same. A hadith in Abu Dawud gives more reward for each fuller form.

entries.meaning: In the name of Allah.
entries.when: Before eating, before wudu, and before starting a task.
entries.note: The Prophet told a boy at his table to mention Allah's name before eating.

entries.meaning: If Allah wills.
entries.when: When you speak about something you plan to do: "See you tomorrow, in sha Allah."
entries.note: The Quran teaches it for plans. It is recommended, not required, and if you forget you can say it when you remember. Some people use it as a soft "maybe". That is a habit, not its meaning, so say it when you really intend to do the thing.

entries.meaning: This is what Allah has willed.
entries.when: When you see or hear something good: a new baby, a new home, someone's progress.
entries.note: The words come from Quran 18:39, which goes on: la quwwata illa billah (there is no power except with Allah). For bad news, use inna lillahi instead.

entries.meaning: All praise belongs to Allah.
entries.when: To give thanks, to answer "How are you?", and after you sneeze.

entries.meaning: Glory be to Allah.
entries.when: As remembrance at any time, including after prayer. Many people also say it when something amazes them.

entries.meaning: I ask Allah's forgiveness.
entries.when: After a slip, when you realise you did something wrong, or as daily remembrance.
entries.note: The Prophet asked for forgiveness more than seventy times a day, so saying it is a normal habit, not an admission of something terrible.

entries.meaning: May Allah reward you with good.
entries.when: To thank someone who has helped you or done you a favour.
entries.reply: Wa iyyak or wa iyyakum (and you too), or wa antum fa jazakumullahu khayran (and may Allah reward you too).
entries.note: A hadith in at-Tirmidhi calls these words the fullest way to thank someone. It is graded hasan.

entries.meaning: May Allah bless you.
entries.note: The words are close to the blessing the Prophet gave at weddings (see the wedding card below). The short reply is common courtesy.

entries.meaning: May Allah have mercy on you.
entries.when: When someone near you sneezes and says Alhamdulillah.
entries.reply: The person who sneezed answers: Yahdikumullah wa yuslihu balakum (may Allah guide you and set your affairs right).
entries.note: All three lines come from one hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari.

entries.meaning: O Allah, answer.
entries.when: After someone makes a dua, and in congregational prayer when the imam finishes Al-Fatihah and says Ameen.
entries.note: Two hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim tell people praying behind the imam to say Ameen when he says it. If you have questions about saying it in your own prayer, ask a teacher.

entries.phrase: Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un
entries.meaning: Surely to Allah we belong and to Him we will return.
entries.when: When you hear of a death or any loss, large or small.
entries.note: The words are from Quran 2:156. A hadith in Sahih Muslim adds a short dua: Allahumma'jurni fi musibati wa akhlif li khayran minha (O Allah, reward me for my loss and give me something better).

entries.phrase: Inna lillahi ma akhadha (comforting someone who is grieving)
entries.arabic: إِنَّ لِلَّهِ مَا أَخَذَ وَلَهُ مَا أَعْطَى
entries.meaning: What Allah takes is His, and what He gives is His. Everything with Him has its set time.
entries.when: To comfort someone after a death.
entries.note: The Prophet sent these words to his daughter when her child was dying, with the advice to be patient and hope for reward. He wept himself, and called his tears mercy. Saying "I am so sorry" and sitting with the family is also right.

entries.phrase: La ba's, tahurun in sha Allah (visiting someone who is ill)
entries.arabic: لَا بَأْسَ طَهُورٌ إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ
entries.meaning: No harm, it is a purification, if Allah wills. This is a literal rendering; Sunnah.com's translation reads "No harm will befall you! May Allah cure you!"
entries.when: When you visit someone who is sick.

entries.phrase: Astawdi'ullaha dinaka (saying goodbye to a traveller)
entries.arabic: أَسْتَوْدِعُ اللَّهَ دِينَكَ وَأَمَانَتَكَ وَخَوَاتِيمَ عَمَلِكَ
entries.meaning: I entrust to Allah your religion, what you are trusted with, and the last of your deeds.
entries.when: When someone is setting off on a journey.
entries.note: The full phrase is Astawdi'ullaha dinaka wa amanataka wa khawatima 'amalik. A hadith in at-Tirmidhi, graded hasan, reports the Prophet saying it.

entries.phrase: Barak Allahu laka wa baraka 'alayka (at a wedding)
entries.arabic: بَارَكَ اللَّهُ لَكَ وَبَارَكَ عَلَيْكَ وَجَمَعَ بَيْنَكُمَا فِي خَيْرٍ
entries.meaning: May Allah bless you, send blessings on you, and bring the two of you together in goodness.
entries.when: To congratulate someone who has just married.
entries.note: The full phrase ends wa jama'a baynakuma fi khayr. It is the Prophet's own congratulation, in a hadith in Abu Dawud graded sahih.

entries.phrase: Eid mubarak, or Taqabbal Allahu minna wa minkum
entries.meaning: Blessed Eid. May Allah accept from us and from you.
entries.reply: The same words back, or Eid mubarak.
entries.note: The Companions greeted each other on Eid with "May Allah accept from us and from you", and any good greeting, including Eid mubarak, is fine. People also say taqabbal Allah (may Allah accept) after someone prays, fasts or gives charity, as a kind wish.

entries.meaning: May Allah send blessings and peace on him. In English, "peace be upon him".
entries.when: When you say, hear or read the name of the Prophet Muhammad.
entries.note: The Quran tells believers to send blessings and peace on the Prophet. The questions and answers page explains the short forms such as SAW and PBUH.

otherWords.title: Words you may hear from other languages
otherWords.intro: Many Muslims in Canada grew up speaking Urdu, Bengali, Persian, Turkish or Arabic at home, and a few everyday words carry over. They are not religious terms, and nobody expects you to use them.

items.meaning: the prayer (salah), in Persian, Urdu, Turkish and Bengali
a fast (sawm), in Persian and Urdu
mum, in Urdu and other South Asian languages
my brother, in Arabic, a friendly word between men
my sister, in Arabic, a friendly word between women
my dear, in Arabic (habibti for a woman), everyday affection
brother, in Urdu, Hindi and Bengali, often added after a name
